sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>
sections.docs:
<docs>
Pi documentation (read only when the user asks about pi itself, its SDK, extensions, themes, skills, or TUI):
- Main documentation: ~/.pi/agent/install/releases/1.4.0/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/README.md
- Additional docs: ~/.pi/agent/install/releases/1.4.0/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/docs
- Examples: ~/.pi/agent/install/releases/1.4.0/node_modules/@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent/examples (extensions, custom tools, SDK)
- When reading pi docs or examples, resolve docs/... under Additional docs and examples/... under Examples, not the current working directory
- When asked about: extensions (docs/extensions.md, examples/extensions/), themes (docs/themes.md), skills (docs/skills.md), prompt templates (docs/prompt-templates.md), TUI components (docs/tui.md), keybindings (docs/keybindings.md), SDK integrations (docs/sdk.md), custom providers (docs/custom-provider.md), adding models (docs/models.md), pi packages (docs/packages.md), environment variables (docs/environment-variables.md), MCP servers (docs/mcp.md), codemode scripts and non-LLM models such as classifiers and image models (docs/codemode.md)
- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)
</docs>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
Make an SVG that, if everyone saw it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Deliver the result as image and/or video files, working in the current directory.
- Save the finished files in ./output/. Only what is in ./output/ is published as the result, so
  ./output/ holds those finished image/video files and nothing else.
- Formats: images as .png, .jpg, .webp, .gif or .svg; videos as .mp4 or .webm. At most 8 files,
  each under 2 MB; videos at most 10 seconds.
- To check your work, look at what you made (a still, a rendered frame, a few frames of the video), and
  save what you look at as .jpg rather than .png: each image you read stays in your context, and a long
  session of large .png files can hit the provider's per-request image limit and end the run.
- Tools available on this machine: python3 3.12.13 (standard library only), node 24.18.0 (no npm packages), ffmpeg 8.1.1, ffprobe 8.1.1. Don't install packages or download anything.
- Keep the code you write to make the files in the working directory (its root, or a subdirectory
  like ./src/, but not in ./output/): it's published as the source. Delete intermediate files such
  as rendered frames when you're done.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- Finish with a short summary of what you made.

content.thinking:
I need to create an SVG that would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

The design must be universally understood and transcendent of language. Kindness, empathy, and environmental care are the leading themes.

Public health, mental wellness, and small acts of kindness are now the leading candidates. The design must be purely visual to bypass language barriers.

The Golden Rule is the strongest candidate. It is the foundation of almost every moral system and would reduce violence and discrimination if universally internalized. Public health messages were rejected as too controversial or preachy. The design must be beautiful, memorable, and emotionally resonant rather than text-heavy.

The "same light" concept is now under consideration. It would show diverse people as connected through hands or shared illumination. A pause-and-reflect moment before speaking or acting is also being explored. The most specific high-impact message is checking on loved ones and telling them they matter, since loneliness and suicide are massive global problems.

This is an art-criticism challenge, so the SVG must function as a standalone artistic piece rather than a purely functional poster. Handwashing and ORS for diarrhea were considered for their statistical lives-saved impact, but they were rejected as too utilitarian and unattractive.

The Overview Effect is now the leading concept. Seeing Earth as one fragile home could increase empathy and environmental concern. This would be a purely visual artistic piece rather than an infographic.

The Overview Effect was rejected as too familiar. A circular composition showing one act of care multiplying through diverse people until it returns larger is now the leading concept. It visually argues that kindness is not zero-sum and compounds.

The "10-second pause" concept is now under consideration to reduce violence. A multilingual "Be kind" message was dismissed as cliché and ineffective. The design must combine universal visual language, emotional beauty, and a clear behavioral nudge. Effective altruism thinking is weighing whether a slight dietary shift could maximize global impact by improving animal welfare and climate outcomes.

The design is now focused on reducing conflict and encouraging help toward strangers. It will remind viewers that the person on the other side is a full human, and it will discourage spreading cruelty online.

The core message is now "They are you, in different circumstances." This recognition of shared humanity would reduce racism, war support, cruelty, and neglect. The visual concept is a circular mandala or human figure where faces merge into one another, titled "The Other Is You."

The design now centers on two hands of different skin tones touching, with radiating scenes showing care passing between people of different ages and appearances. Earth appears as a thin ring. A single line of text will use simple symbols rather than language. An animated SVG is being considered alongside a rendered video.

I have rsvg-convert, Chrome, ffmpeg, and qlmanage available.

I'm designing an SVG meant to be visually striking and universally impactful. The goal is a high-leverage message that transcends language barriers and leaves a lasting impression.

The core message is "The person in front of you is as real as you are." This single mental model could shift millions of daily decisions and reduce suffering across the globe.

Dehumanization drives war, cruelty, and exploitation. The image should also nudge three secondary behaviors: repair before escalation, give the benefit of the doubt, and treat attention as a gift rather than a weapon.

The image will be a large human face built entirely from tiny scenes of people helping, working, and caring. It forces the viewer to recognize their own reflection in "the other," producing the feeling directly rather than lecturing.

The composition is now a split mirror: one side shows the viewer, the other shows another person with the same expression and light in their eyes. A thin vertical line between them represents shared heartbeat or light. The design will be pure visual with no text to avoid language barriers.

content.thinking:
System fonts are available for SVG rendering via rsvg-convert.

The concept is a visual mirror that shows the viewer as the person they are about to harm. It prompts empathy before action.

The plan is shifting to a short silent animation. It will show a person first as an abstract category, then reveal their face and hands, ending with the viewer's hand meeting theirs. This sequence is meant to break dehumanization and spark recognition.

The animation is titled "The Same Light" and runs nine seconds. It opens with two silhouettes separated by a wall. A small light appears between them. As it grows, their faces reveal different ages and skin tones. The wall becomes transparent. One offers bread or water. The light then spreads to a ring of figures around the world.

The primary deliverable is an SVG image. A PNG or JPG may be rendered as well. The final frame shows the Earth as a circle of people holding light, with words that need no translation.

The plan is shifting back to a static poster. The title will be "AS REAL AS YOU." It will be a vertical image sized for mobile phones, around 1080 by 1350 pixels. A generator script will be written in the working directory and the finished SVG saved to ./output/.

The poster dimensions are now set at 1400 by 1800 or 1600 by 2000 pixels. A night-to-dawn scene will be the background. The center will feature two people sitting across a small table from an elevated angle. To avoid looking like clipart, the figures will be symbolic and painterly rather than cartoonish. A hands-only composition is also being considered.

The design is now a circular arrangement of hands. Offered and received hands form pairs around the center, linked by threads of light. The central palm faces the viewer, its lines forming a map or river system that suggests the world is in one hand. This symbolizes that the same life belongs to everyone.

The central palm will be large and open, its lines filled with tiny scenes of human life. The skin tone is ambiguous or gradient, so it reads as every person's hand. A ring of small text in many languages will sit around the wrist. The chosen sentence is "They feel it as much as you do."

The golden rule is too familiar to move people. The focus is shifting to behavioral specificity drawn from research on what actually changes behavior.

Four concrete daily actions are now the focus: assume strangers are having a hard day and treat them gently, share a little with someone who lacks, listen fully to one person today, and refuse to pass on cruelty. These micro-actions are chosen for their global scale and immediate impact.

The message is now "See them. Then be gentle." or the sharper reminder that both the stranger and you can be hurt, so choose the gentler thing. The design will follow Saul Bass, Polish poster school, Japanese graphic design, and Milton Glaser's "I love NY" in aiming for a single bold symbol that survives moments of anger, scrolling, driving, and politics.

The design is now a single pair of eyes. Each pupil reflects a tiny life: a room, a child, rain at a window, a meal. The background is deep indigo-brown like dusk. The eyes are luminous and calm, not frightening.

The irises will shift through many colors at once, suggesting every person's eyes. Each pupil will reflect a tiny scene: a kitchen light and waiting figure on the left, hands holding a child or a person looking out a window on the right. A single serif line below the eyes reads "Someone is home in there." A second instruction beneath it was considered but rejected as too much.

The message is now a single line: "Someone is home in there." It frames the core idea that every person has an inner life as vivid as our own, which is the philosophical heart of moral circle expansion. A second panel or lower third for translation is also being considered.

Four small pictograms are being considered to show the concrete actions that follow from the eye message: offering a hand, sharing food, listening, and speaking softly. The poster may instead use a quiet band of eight languages for the sentence itself.

The language list now includes Bengali, Portuguese, Russian, Japanese, Indonesian, and Urdu. The translator is uncertain about the accuracy of these translations. Incorrect translations would be harmful. The plan is to either use only known translations or keep the message purely visual.

Draft translations for Spanish and French are being weighed, but Chinese, Arabic, and Hindi remain too uncertain. The plan is shifting to a purely visual image with one carefully chosen English line and universal symbols, avoiding any translated text.

The double-exposure silhouette risks looking like a 2015 stock template. The chest-window metaphor is more original and will be refined through craft alone. A viewer reflection is also being considered to increase the image's world-impact.

The viewer reflection idea is deferred until the base image is rendered. The output directory will be created first. The final format will be 1200×1600 vertical, optimized for mobile sharing.

The video will be rendered at 720×960 to keep the file under two megabytes while the SVG stays at full resolution. Text in the published SVG must be converted to paths or fonts embedded, since system fonts are not guaranteed to exist on every viewer's machine.

The raster output is safe because rsvg-convert renders text as pixels. Embedding Apple system fonts in the SVG is risky due to copyright and licensing concerns, so converting text to paths remains the safer approach.

The headline will be drawn as hand-drawn paths. A minimal TTF parser could extract outlines from system fonts, but that is too complex for simple glyphs.

A minimal TTF parser will extract glyph outlines and convert text to SVG paths.

Georgia and Arial are single TTF files, unlike Charter which is in a TTC. The SVG will be self-contained with text converted to paths so it renders correctly anywhere.

The converter will parse TrueType glyph headers and coordinate flags to reconstruct SVG path data.

TrueType coordinates are relative deltas. On-curve points become SVG anchors. Off-curve points become quadratic bezier controls. Consecutive off-curve points imply an on-curve midpoint. The algorithm traces contours as lines or quadratic curves.

cmap will map Unicode characters to glyph IDs using formats 4 and 12. hmtx and head tables provide advance widths and unitsPerEm. Kerning may be parsed from Georgia's kern table or GPOS for a polished headline.

Georgia and Georgia Italic will serve as the sole typefaces for a unified serif poster. Avenir Next is a TTC collection, so it was set aside.

Small caps will be faked by scaling uppercase letters and adding letter-spacing. A PNG or JPG fallback will be rendered with rsvg-convert to preserve the canonical visual, but the SVG remains the primary deliverable.

Hand-drawing the word "Someone is home in there." was considered as a more artistic alternative to parsing Georgia, but it would likely look worse than the font. The Python TTF parser is now being written, starting with the offset table and table directory.

The parser will also handle TrueType Collections. It will be tested on a simple glyph before building the poster.

The poster will show a silhouette of a calm person standing in a dark city at night with scattered lit windows. The still image is the priority; animation will follow only if the static version is strong enough.

The silhouette's chest contains a warm window revealing a small room with a lamp, table, two cups, and a plant. The person's eyes glow with the same inner light. Other figures on the street each carry a tiny lit window. The wet pavement reflects all the lights into a scattered constellation of homes. Quiet type will read "Someone is home in there." and "Be gentle. You are in there too."

The figure will stand with both hands relaxed at their sides. They will not raise a palm or gesture. The stillness itself conveys dignity and invites quiet observation.

The poster will invite eye contact as the central action. The inner lamp and the outer eyes will share the same warm color for a visual rhyme. The face will be built from carefully tuned SVG paths and refined through several iterations.

The poster will be rendered at 1200×1600 pixels. A smaller JPG preview at roughly 800×1067 with quality 70 will be used for review to avoid hitting file limits. The final image will be saved as a high-resolution JPG. A ten-second video animation is planned for after the still image is complete.

The generator script will live in `src/`. Only the SVG and any video will be placed in `output/`; a duplicate JPG is unnecessary.

Previews will be saved to `./preview/` or `/tmp` and deleted afterward, keeping `output/` free of temporary files. A static SVG is the safer primary deliverable because SMIL animation has inconsistent browser support; video will remain a separate file. Node.js string templates may be used for SVG generation.

Everything will be built in Python. The face will be refined by rendering only the upper portion first, then adjusting before finishing the rest. A more original compositional twist is being considered to elevate the poster from good to memorable art.

A recursive echo is being considered for the chest window: inside the room, a tiny figure with a window would reveal another person standing in the rain. This would reinforce the idea that everyone contains everyone else. The risk is that the detail might be too small to read, so it will only be attempted if the room remains visually balanced.

A radial gradient from the hero window will spill light onto the nearest small figure, making kindness a visible action. The palette is now fixed: deep midnight blues for the sky and buildings, charcoal grays for the coat, and soft face shadows.

The palette is now fully defined. Warm browns and beiges will shade the face, eyes, and coat. The window frame, room walls, floor, lamp, plant pot, and cups each have specific tones. Text will use pale grays and browns. The figure will be large and centered, with its head at y=250, chin at y=560, and coat extending to y=1100.

The figure will occupy 850 pixels of the 1600-pixel canvas, leaving 200 pixels for the sky and 400 for the text. The chest window will be 220 pixels tall. The head will measure 320 by 240 pixels, with its eyes placed at y=400.

The figure's eyes will sit at y=415, accounting for hair volume above the skull. A subtle grain filter will be added to the SVG, though it may be skipped if rasterization is too slow or inconsistent across renderers.

The grain effect will be replaced by 200 faint noise circles at 0.03 opacity, avoiding filter dependency entirely. A soft radial vignette will darken the edges. The SVG title metadata will be included. The first draft of the generator script is now being written.

The figure's side hand will be drawn as a rounded palm with a separate thumb, plus overlapping finger shapes. The coat will feature a notched lapel that catches a thin moon highlight on the left and warm inner light from the chest window.

The static SVG will stand alone and carry all text, while the MP4 video will serve as the experience of looking again. Planning is complete and the generator script is ready to be written.

The room will use a thick wooden frame with visible miter corners or simple molding. A plant will sit on the sill and the curtain will be tied back. The window will appear as a physical framed object attached to the coat, offset by a small shadow, or as a flush niche with stone or wood lining.

The chest window will be flush and integrated into the coat, not a detached object with a drop shadow. This keeps the metaphor of the figure as a living home rather than a picture frame.

The figure will be rendered as a flat architectural shape rather than realistic anatomy. The face and eyes keep the human identity, while the coat body reads as a house-like window. Headline text will be 86 pixels in Georgia Regular, the italic line 80 pixels in Georgia Italic, the subtitle 28 pixels in Georgia Regular, and the colophon 16 pixels with extra letter-spacing. Kern tables will be read to improve glyph spacing.

The text is purely ASCII, so composite glyphs and complex GPOS tables are unnecessary. Only basic glyph pairs need kerning.

Roughly three hundred noise ellipses should remain well under the two-megabyte limit. A comment may be added to the SVG source.

The phrase "in there." will sit just below the figure in the warm lamp color. The period may become a tiny lit window icon, or the dot of the "i" could serve as a small window. A small window symbol between the headline and subline is enough. The text layout is being refined.

The text layout now places a 14-pixel glowing window icon beside the headline. The final line names three specific human-caused sufferings: the raised hand, the harsh word, and turning back. These cover violence, verbal cruelty, and indifference. They represent actions that individuals can choose to stop in the moment.

The final six-line text layout is now fixed. The headline reads "Someone is home" and "in there." A small window mark sits between them. The subline will be "Look again. Be gentle." or a shorter variant. The last line names the three specific human-caused sufferings. Lines four and five may be merged.

The poster will pair a negative warning with a positive action. The final line will read "Leave them warmer than you found them," turning the warm window metaphor into an actionable duty.

The final text is now fixed. The headline reads "Someone is home" and "in there." The last line reads "Leave them warmer than you found them." This phrasing is more original and memorable than a simple warning. It carries both a negative prohibition and a positive duty. It applies to every person met, including the viewer themselves.

The poster is now a four-line composition. The colophon is dropped to avoid clutter, leaving only the headline, the warm-window line, and the final action line. The last two lines may use a lighter weight or smaller size.

The final line "You are in there too." is restored. It recognizes the viewer's own inner life and addresses private suffering like suicide and self-harm, which a simple warning would miss.

The Python generator script is being organized with a dedicated face-drawing function and tweakable constants. A slightly illustrative, three-quarter-view face is being considered for more life.

The figure will be nearly symmetrical, like a Byzantine icon. A single tiny asymmetry will keep it alive: a different catchlight, a stray hair strand, or the plant on one side of the window. The room itself is asymmetric, creating a balance between sacred and domestic.

The figure will be symmetric, with a soft warm glow on the inner ear to humanize it. Subtle cheekbone hints and a soft shadow under the chin add life without looking like a cartoon. The neck will be visible between the hair and collar, lit from below by the window glow. This unusual key light from below makes the image distinctive.

The face will be lit by a warm key light from the chest window and a cool moon light from above. The eyes will sit in the shadow band between them, with catchlights to keep them readable. This creates a cinematic effect of a face warmed by the home within. Gradients will handle the lighting.

A radial gradient was rejected for the face. A linear gradient from cool shadow to warmest amber will run from top to bottom. A soft warm ellipse will be overlaid on the chin and neck area.

A 12 fps video would feel too jerky for a contemplative piece. Full resolution at 24 fps is preferred, with a smaller 720×960 render for the video to save time. A child inside the chest would feel creepy, so the figure will be an adult or androgynous person reading a book. The crowd already includes children outside, keeping the vulnerable represented without adding a child to the interior.

The warm amber on the dark night background is confirmed as high-contrast and readable. A font parser and first visual draft will be written next, with rapid iteration planned. The coat silhouette will use a subtle darker line at the arm-to-torso junction to avoid looking like a sack. The files will be named `someone-is-home.svg` and `someone-is-home.mp4`. No license or README will be added to the output directory.

A square crop was considered but rejected to keep the output to two files. Georgia will be the main font for reliability and beauty, with Arial as a fallback for the small line.

A helper is being written to convert TrueType contours into SVG quadratic Bézier paths. It interpolates missing on-curve points between off-curve control points so the glyph shape closes properly.

The contour-to-path converter now rotates the expanded point list so the first point is on-curve. It maps font coordinates to SVG pixels with a Y-flip, then begins assembling the SVG path string.

The contour-to-path converter now assembles SVG quadratic Bézier commands for off-curve control points and straight lines for on-curve points, then closes the path with a Z command.

The contour-to-path loop is being refined to match the standard TrueType specification. The algorithm now uses a `start` variable and an explicit index, drawing straight lines for on-curve points and quadratic Béziers for off-curve control points that pair with the next on-curve point.

Wraparound logic is being added to the contour-to-path loop so curves that close back to the start point are handled correctly. The chest window is being refined to 190 by 230 pixels. It will read as a window rather than a hole thanks to its strong frame. The head size is being adjusted so the figure does not compete with the focal point while keeping the eyes visible.

The eye will travel from the eyes to the window and then to the text. A table with legs will sit below. Two small cups will sit on the table: one held by the figure and one empty across from it. This suggests hospitality without adding a plate or bread.

A small picture will hang on the back wall. Inside it will be abstract warm and cool vertical bands. This evokes a memory of outside without looking like a smudge.

A deep indigo curtain will hang on the left side of the room, pulled back with a small band. It echoes the outside night while contrasting with the warm interior. The room stays fully enclosed; no moon or steam will appear.

Reflections will appear on the left and right sides of the coat hem, with a glow extending from the bottom center into the text area. Rain specks will land on the shoulders. """Minimal TrueType outliner: ASCII text to SVG paths. No dependencies."""

import struct
from dataclasses import dataclass


def _u16(data, off):
    return struct.unpack_from(">H", data, off)[0]


def _i16(data, off):
    return struct.unpack_from(">h", data, off)[0]


def _u32(data, off):
    return struct.unpack_from(">I", data, off)[0]


@dataclass
class Font:
    data: bytes
    tables: dict
    units: int
    glyph_id: callable
    num_glyphs: int
    loca: list
    advances: list
    lsbs: list
    kern: dict


def _tables(data, start):
    num = _u16(data, start + 4)
    tables = {}
    off = start + 12
    for _ in range(num):
        tag = data[off : off + 4].decode("latin1")
        tables[tag] = (_u32(data, off + 8), _u32(data, off + 12))
        off += 16
    return tables


def _slice(data, tables, tag):
    off, length = tables[tag]
    return data[off : off + length], off


def _parse_cmap(data, tables):
    raw, base = _slice(data, tables, "cmap")
    num = _u16(raw, 2)
    best = None
    for i in range(num):
        plat, enc, offset = struct.unpack_from(">HHI", raw, 4 + i * 8)
        fmt = _u16(raw, offset)
        # Prefer Unicode BMP or full, then Windows Unicode BMP.
        score = -1
        if plat == 0 and fmt in (4, 12):
            score = 3
        elif plat == 3 and enc == 1 and fmt == 4:
            score = 2
        elif plat == 3 and enc == 10 and fmt == 12:
            score = 3
        if score > (best[0] if best else -1):
            best = (score, fmt, offset)
    if not best:
        raise RuntimeError("no usable cmap")
    _, fmt, offset = best
    if fmt == 4:
        return _cmap4(raw, offset)
    if fmt == 12:
        return _cmap12(raw, offset)
    raise RuntimeError(f"unsupported cmap format {fmt}")


def _cmap4(raw, offset):
    seg_count = _u16(raw, offset + 6) // 2
    p = offset + 14
    end_count = struct.unpack_from(f">{seg_count}H", raw, p)
    p += seg_count * 2 + 2
    start_count = struct.unpack_from(f">{seg_count}H", raw, p)
    p += seg_count * 2
    id_delta = struct.unpack_from(f">{seg_count}h", raw, p)
    p += seg_count * 2
    range_off_pos = p
    id_range = struct.unpack_from(f">{seg_count}H", raw, p)

    def glyph_id(code):
        for i in range(seg_count):
            if start_count[i] <= code <= end_count[i]:
                if id_range[i] == 0:
                    return (code + id_delta[i]) & 0xFFFF
                pos = range_off_pos + i * 2 + id_range[i] + (code - start_count[i]) * 2
                g = _u16(raw, pos)
                if g == 0:
                    return 0
                return (g + id_delta[i]) & 0xFFFF
        return 0

    return glyph_id


def _cmap12(raw, offset):
    n = _u32(raw, offset + 12)
    groups = []
    p = offset + 16
    for _ in range(n):
        start, end, glyph = struct.unpack_from(">III", raw, p)
        groups.append((start, end, glyph))
        p += 12

    def glyph_id(code):
        lo, hi = 0, len(groups) - 1
        while lo <= hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            start, end, glyph = groups[mid]
            if code < start:
                hi = mid - 1
            elif code > end:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                return glyph + (code - start)
        return 0

    return glyph_id


def _parse_loca(data, tables, units_head, num_glyphs):
    head, _ = _slice(data, tables, "head")
    loc_format = _i16(head, 50)
    loca_raw, _ = _slice(data, tables, "loca")
    loca = []
    if loc_format == 0:
        for i in range(num_glyphs + 1):
            loca.append(_u16(loca_raw, i * 2) * 2)
    else:
        for i in range(num_glyphs + 1):
            loca.append(_u32(loca_raw, i * 4))
    return loca


def _parse_hmtx(data, tables, num_glyphs):
    hhea, _ = _slice(data, tables, "hhea")
    n_metrics = _u16(hhea, 34)
    raw, _ = _slice(data, tables, "hmtx")
    advances = []
    lsbs = []
    for i in range(n_metrics):
        advances.append(_u16(raw, i * 4))
        lsbs.append(_i16(raw, i * 4 + 2))
    last = advances[-1]
    extra = num_glyphs - n_metrics
    p = n_metrics * 4
    for i in range(extra):
        advances.append(last)
        lsbs.append(_i16(raw, p + i * 2))
    return advances, lsbs


def _parse_kern(data, tables):
    kern = {}
    if "kern" not in tables:
        return kern
    raw, _ = _slice(data, tables, "kern")
    if len(raw) < 4:
        return kern
    version, n_tables = struct.unpack_from(">HH", raw, 0)
    p = 4
    for _ in range(n_tables):
        if p + 6 > len(raw):
            break
        st_ver, length, coverage = struct.unpack_from(">HHH", raw, p)
        fmt = coverage & 0xFF
        if fmt == 0 and length >= 14:
            n_pairs = _u16(raw, p + 6)
            q = p + 14
            for _ in range(n_pairs):
                left, right, value = struct.unpack_from(">HHh", raw, q)
                kern[(left, right)] = value
                q += 6
        p += length
    return kern


def load_font(path):
    data = open(path, "rb").read()
    if data[:4] == b"ttcf":
        raise RuntimeError("TTC not supported; pass a single-face TTF")
    tables = _tables(data, 0)
    head, _ = _slice(data, tables, "head")
    units = _u16(head, 18)
    maxp, _ = _slice(data, tables, "maxp")
    num_glyphs = _u16(maxp, 4)
    glyph_id = _parse_cmap(data, tables)
    loca = _parse_loca(data, tables, units, num_glyphs)
    advances, lsbs = _parse_hmtx(data, tables, num_glyphs)
    kern = _parse_kern(data, tables)
    return Font(data, tables, units, glyph_id, num_glyphs, loca, advances, lsbs, kern)


def _glyph_contours(font, gid):
    if gid <= 0 or gid >= len(font.loca) - 1:
        return []
    start = font.loca[gid]
    end = font.loca[gid + 1]
    if end <= start:
        return []
    glyf, gbase = _slice(font.data, font.tables, "glyf")
    # loca offsets are relative to glyf table
    p = start
    n_contours = _i16(glyf, p)
    if n_contours < 0:
        return _composite_contours(font, glyf, p)
    if n_contours == 0:
        return []
    p += 10
    ends = [ _u16(glyf, p + i * 2) for i in range(n_contours) ]
    p += n_contours * 2
    inst_len = _u16(glyf, p)
    p += 2 + inst_len
    n_points = ends[-1] + 1
    flags = []
    while len(flags) < n_points:
        f = glyf[p]
        p += 1
        flags.append(f)
        if f & 0x08:
            rep = glyf[p]
            p += 1
            flags.extend([f] * rep)
    xs = []
    x = 0
    for f in flags:
        if f & 0x02:
            dx = glyf[p]
            p += 1
            if not (f & 0x10):
                dx = -dx
        elif f & 0x10:
            dx = 0
        else:
            dx = _i16(glyf, p)
            p += 2
        x += dx
        xs.append(x)
    ys = []
    y = 0
    for f in flags:
        if f & 0x04:
            dy = glyf[p]
            p += 1
            if not (f & 0x20):
                dy = -dy
        elif f & 0x20:
            dy = 0
        else:
            dy = _i16(glyf, p)
            p += 2
        y += dy
        ys.append(y)
    on = [(f & 1) != 0 for f in flags]
    contours = []
    s = 0
    for e in ends:
        contours.append(list(zip(xs[s : e + 1], ys[s : e + 1], on[s : e + 1])))
        s = e + 1
    return contours


def _composite_contours(font, glyf, p):
    # Walk composite glyph, applying translation (and simple scale if present).
    contours = []
    p += 10
    while True:
        flags = _u16(glyf, p)
        gid = _u16(glyf, p + 2)
        p += 4
        if flags & 0x01:  # ARG_1_AND_2_ARE_WORDS
            dx, dy = _i16(glyf, p), _i16(glyf, p + 2)
            p += 4
        else:
            dx = struct.unpack_from(">b", glyf, p)[0]
            dy = struct.unpack_from(">b", glyf, p + 1)[0]
            p += 2
        scale_x = scale_y = 1.0
        if flags & 0x08:  # WE_HAVE_A_SCALE
            scale_x = scale_y = _i16(glyf, p) / 16384.0
            p += 2
        elif flags & 0x40:  # WE_HAVE_AN_X_AND_Y_SCALE
            scale_x = _i16(glyf, p) / 16384.0
            scale_y = _i16(glyf, p + 2) / 16384.0
            p += 4
        elif flags & 0x80:  # WE_HAVE_A_TWO_BY_TWO
            p += 8  # ignore transform, still place by dx/dy
        for cont in _glyph_contours(font, gid):
            moved = [(px * scale_x + dx, py * scale_y + dy, on) for px, py, on in cont]
            contours.append(moved)
        if not (flags & 0x20):  # MORE_COMPONENTS
            break
    return contours


def _contour_path(contour, scale, ox, oy):
    if not contour:
        return ""
    pts = [(x, y, on) for x, y, on in contour]
    # Insert implied on-curve points between consecutive off-curve points.
    expanded = []
    n = len(pts)
    for i in range(n):
        expanded.append(pts[i])
        x1, y1, on1 = pts[i]
        x2, y2, on2 = pts[(i + 1) % n]
        if not on1 and not on2:
            expanded.append(((x1 + x2) / 2, (y1 + y2) / 2, True))
    # Rotate to an on-curve start.
    idx = next(i for i, p in enumerate(expanded) if p[2])
    expanded = expanded[idx:] + expanded[:idx]

    def tx(x, y):
        return ox + x * scale, oy - y * scale

    def fmt(x, y):
        return f"{x:.2f} {y:.2f}"

    sx, sy = tx(*expanded[0][:2])
    parts = [f"M {fmt(sx, sy)}"]
    i = 0
    m = len(expanded)
    # Walk until we have consumed every point once and closed.
    seen = 0
    while seen < m:
        j = (i + 1) % m
        if expanded[j][2]:
            x, y = tx(*expanded[j][:2])
            parts.append(f"L {fmt(x, y)}")
            i = j
            seen += 1
        else:
            cx, cy = tx(*expanded[j][:2])
            k = (j + 1) % m
            if expanded[k][2]:
                ex, ey = tx(*expanded[k][:2])
                end_i = k
            else:
                # Should not happen after implied-point insertion.
                mx = (expanded[j][0] + expanded[k][0]) / 2
                my = (expanded[j][1] + expanded[k][1]) / 2
                ex, ey = tx(mx, my)
                end_i = j  # stay; next loop handles k
            parts.append(f"Q {fmt(cx, cy)} {fmt(ex, ey)}")
            step = (end_i - i) % m
            i = end_i
            seen += step if step else m
        if i == 0:
            break
    parts.append("Z")
    return " ".join(parts)


def text_path(font, text, size, x, y, anchor="start", fill="#000", letter_spacing=0, extra=""):
    """Return an SVG <path> element. (x, y) is the anchor point on the baseline."""
    scale = size / font.units
    glyphs = []
    pen = 0.0
    prev = None
    for ch in text:
        gid = font.glyph_id(ord(ch))
        adv = font.advances[gid] if gid < len(font.advances) else font.units // 3
        k = 0
        if prev is not None:
            k = font.kern.get((prev, gid), 0)
        glyphs.append((gid, pen + k))
        pen += adv + k + letter_spacing * font.units / size
        prev = gid
    width = pen - (letter_spacing * font.units / size if text else 0)
    width_px = width * scale
    if anchor == "middle":
        origin = x - width_px / 2
    elif anchor == "end":
        origin = x - width_px
    else:
        origin = x
    d_parts = []
    for gid, gx in glyphs:
        contours = _glyph_contours(font, gid)
        ox = origin + gx * scale
        for cont in contours:
            d_parts.append(_contour_path(cont, scale, ox, y))
    d = " ".join(p for p in d_parts if p)
    return f'<path fill="{fill}" d="{d}" {extra}/>', width_px


def measure(font, text, size, letter_spacing=0):
    _, w = text_path(font, text, size, 0, 0, letter_spacing=letter_spacing)
    return w

Georgia outlines are accurate. Kerning is missing, but the spacing looks professional and acceptable.

Now building the full poster SVG. The canvas is 1200×1600 with a dark gradient sky background.

Adding a golden radial glow and a dark vignette to the poster background.

Adding soft blur filters to the SVG definitions. Stars will be randomly seeded in the upper half of the sky, avoiding the head area. The crescent moon is being drawn as a masked path instead of simple circles.

The crescent moon mask is now defined with a white circle and a black cutout. The moon itself will be a soft, low-opacity glow circle with a blur filter.

The crescent moon is now drawn as a masked circle with a soft glow. Buildings are being carefully positioned to frame the figure. The left side has four towers of varying heights and colors. The right side mirrors them with slight differences. Windows will be added to some buildings.

Edge highlights will be added to the moon side of buildings. The figure head is being drawn as a precise SVG path centered at x=600, with carefully curved jaw lines.

The head spans 284 pixels, roughly 24% of the canvas width. Its width-to-shoulder ratio is about 0.55, slightly larger than typical proportions. This oversized head is a deliberate poster convention to keep the face and eyes prominent.

The hair will be drawn as a cap ellipse with sideburns. SVG does not easily support subtractive masking, so the hair will simply be layered on top of the face.

The hair is being drawn as a rounded cap path that overlaps the face. It curves concavely at the forehead to keep the face visible, with sides dropping to y=390. A slight volume bump and a cool left-side highlight stroke are planned. Ears will be added next.

Ears are being drawn as curved C-shapes and will overlap the sides of the head. The neck is being sketched with a warm gradient. A coat silhouette is next.

The coat is being sketched as a knee-length overcoat with an A-line silhouette. The left arm will curve inward at the elbow to show hands in pockets. Shoulder peaks and hem points are mapped on both sides for symmetry. The SVG path is now being drafted.

The coat path is now fully drafted with smooth curves and a symmetrical hem. Lapels are being added as triangular shapes that fold outward from the neck, with a highlight on the outer edge. The window will sit below the V-shaped lapel frame.

The coat is being simplified to a clean, graphic silhouette. Lapels are dropped to avoid looking like a bad fashion drawing. A subtle center line or simple collar band will frame the neck instead.

The coat will use a radial gradient from warm dark near the window to cool dark at the edges. Pocket welts will suggest hands in pockets without drawing them. A single button may sit below the window.

A thin left-side stroke in #3a4a62 will highlight the figure's contour. A soft shadow ellipse will sit under the chin on the neck. The eyes are being drawn as almond-shaped paths with precise control points, centered at (552, 430) and (648, 430).

The eye shape is being refined into a symmetric almond with quadratic Bezier curves. The upper lid will be a darker crescent overlay covering the top third of the eye. The iris is placed slightly below center at (550, 434) with a pupil and two catchlights: a warm dot and a cool one. The upper lid stroke will be 1.5 pixels dark brown, while the lower lid will be thinner and more transparent.

Lashes are being skipped to keep the face clean and universal. The brow is drawn as a thin, relaxed arch with a slight upward curve, positioned about twenty pixels above the eyes.

A faint under-eye shadow will add subtle warmth without looking sad. The nose bridge gets a thin pale highlight, and the tip gets a soft dark shadow. Nostrils may be removed if they look like dirty spots.

The mouth is being drawn as a small, soft curve with a darker outline and a faint warm highlight. Cheeks will be added as subtle warm ellipses at low opacity for a hint of life. A soft warm light will sit under the chin.

The window is being designed as a centered object with a dark frame, a gold inner line, and a wood-grained sill. The neck warm light is being placed at (600, 620) to create a soft glow connecting the figure to the window.

The window interior is being designed in local coordinates within a clipPath group. The back wall will use a warm gradient from cream to gold. The floor will be a brown polygon with a lighter central ellipse for a lamp glow. A baseboard line will sit at y=155.

The lamp interior is being detailed with a dark cord, a cream shade with a darker top edge, and an inner shadow. A warm glow ellipse will sit at the bulb, with a faint light cone falling toward the table.

A small picture frame is being added to the window sill. It will have a dark wood frame, a cream mat, and a tiny landscape image showing sky above a warm ground.

A tiny white moon will sit inside the picture frame to echo the real moon outside. The window interior is being filled with a night-blue curtain and a gold tie-back. A warm brown table will sit beneath the lamp.

The figure's legs are drawn as thin brown rectangles. A shadow will sit under the table on the floor.

Two white cups are placed near the table. One is filled with cream and has a dark inner ellipse for the opening. The other is empty and slightly smaller, positioned to the left as a "room for you" gesture.

The chair back is a dark wood rectangle behind the figure.

The chair seat is drawn as a thin brown rectangle. The figure body will be a warm dark silhouette in #3a2820 rather than a black one, because a dark shape against the warm wall reads more clearly at small size. A warm rim light on the lamp side will add subtle definition.

The figure's head is a small dark circle. A warm crescent rim light will sit on the left shoulder to suggest lamplight. A curved arm stroke will reach toward the cup at x=90. The interior width of 186 pixels is being checked to avoid crowding.

The room composition is balanced: curtain on the left, picture, lamp center-left, table with cups, and figure on the right. A plant is being added to the window sill outside the clip path. It has a dark brown pot with a rim ellipse. Four rotated leaves in varying greens will extend up over the glass and leftward to break the rectangular frame.

A diagonal glass sheen and five raindrops will sit on the window to sell the illusion of a real pane. A warm glow behind the window will use two blurred ellipses at different opacities. A soft spill of warm amber will rest on the coat beneath the window.

A blurred vertical reflection streak will sit on the street below the coat, fading from warm amber at the top to transparent. Smaller reflections will appear under the crowd lights. Distant people will be drawn along a ground line at y=1000, positioned behind and beside the hero.

Crowd figures will be placed outside the hero's silhouette to avoid overlap. Some will partially hide behind the coat for depth. Left-side crowd positions are being mapped with feet at y=980 and y=1000.

The left-side crowd now includes a child holding hands with an adult, a figure close to the hero, and a seated person on a low building step. The right side holds a taller figure, an older person with a cane, and two smaller figures. A Python helper function is being drafted to generate each figure from head size, height, and window position.

The body path will be drawn as a vertical rectangle with a warm chest window. Body widths will vary slightly for each figure, and some will carry a scarf line, a small side bag, or a cane. The child figure will have a larger head ratio at 0.22. A short connecting line will sit between the hands of the two figures holding hands. Crowd windows will use a warm amber fill with a bright inner core, starting at zero opacity for the animation.

Every person in the crowd will be clearly lit, with only a slight dimming for one figure to suggest a quieter hour. Building windows may stay dark to show unoccupied rooms, but no person should appear empty. The message is that every figure has an inner life. Text baseline positions are now being planned.

The text layout is now fixed. "Someone is home" and "in there." sit at y=1268 and y=1358 in warm cream. A tiny divider sits at y=1390. "Leave them warmer" and "than you found them." appear at y=1455 and y=1502 in smaller warm amber. "You are in there too." sits at y=1555 in small italic. The final baseline lands near 1563, leaving only a thin margin before the 1600-pixel height limit.

The text block is being slightly tightened to add breathing room. Baselines shift up by a few pixels, and the two larger headings drop from 78px to 72px. The smaller lines scale down to 34px and 18px. These are final placements for now; they will be fine-tuned after seeing the result.

Headline letter-spacing is being set to 0.8 pixels for a poster-like openness. The final line will use 1.5 letter-spacing as a whispered afterthought. The face will be rendered early so the full poster can be built and then iterated visually.

The symmetrical face will stay as a mask-like icon, balanced by the room's asymmetry. Pupils will sit centered in each eye for a direct gaze. Catchlights will sit low in the irises because the window sits below the eyes.

The moon sits in the upper right of the image, so it falls on the figure's left side. The window light from below will sit lower in each iris as the main catchlight. A second warm catchlight will sit higher on the left side of each eye.

A thin warm stroke will sit on the lower lid to echo the window light. A faint warm gradient will soften the lower half of each sclera. Sparse circles will provide grain for a print feel without relying on turbulence.

Vignette is prioritized over grain. Sparse dust particles were considered but rejected as too dirty. Foreground rain streaks will be larger and softer than the main background rain for depth. The rain color is set to #b7c3d0 at 13% opacity.

Rain will sit only behind the figure and on the coat shoulders, never on the face or window. The wet ground is a horizontal band from y=1090 to y=1250, fading from #121820 at the horizon to #0c1014 at the bottom with a faint sheen line at y=1105 and stroke #2a3544 at 40% opacity. Blurred vertical rectangles will reflect building windows onto the street.

The lower third before the text will feature a dark mirror of the lights. The horizon line will stay flat and graphic rather than using perspective, keeping the composition poster-like.

The style is defined as a contemporary gouache poster with flat shapes, soft gradients, and controlled detail. Most elements are filled rather than stroked to avoid a coloring-book look. The figure will have no black outlines; separation comes from value and a subtle left-side rim light in #6a7c94 at 35% opacity along the head, shoulder, and arm contour.

A warm amber rim light will wrap the right lower coat and cheek at 25% opacity. The code will be modular so layout numbers can be tuned from the top. A small key hanging beside the curtain was considered but rejected as noise.

Shoes inside the room were considered but rejected as clutter. A faint shadow on the back wall will anchor the figure in space. The poster is being written now, with animation groups structured for parameterized opacity.

The first frame will show only the silhouette. The dark head shape must read as a person on its own. Facial features and the warm window glow will fade in afterward for a reveal effect.

The window frame will remain dark in the initial silhouette so the light reveal feels magical and intentional. The window can fade in entirely rather than appearing from nothing.

A title element will be added. The window must read as a body interior rather than a background window. It will overlap the coat completely, with the coat silhouette surrounding it on all sides and the glow spilling onto the garment. A shadow on the coat will hide any background showing through. Shoulders will be wide enough to frame the window fully.

The window is fixed at 210 pixels wide and sits at y=750, just below the chin. The coat path spans x=365 to x=835 at that height, leaving 130 pixels of garment on each side of the frame. This keeps the window clearly inset as a chest interior rather than a belly window. The heart-level placement reinforces the metaphor that the heart is a room without using a literal heart symbol.

A heartbeat symbol was rejected as too cute. The lamp will serve as the life sign instead.

The inner figure will be drawn with clear silhouette rules: a distinct head, a neck gap or shoulder slope, and a seated posture with a chair back. The head will be slightly oversized relative to the body so the figure remains recognizable even at small scale.

The inner figure will be drawn in profile facing left toward the lamp and second cup. A profile silhouette reads instantly as a person even at small scale, whereas a frontal view might look like an ambiguous dark blob.

The inner figure's profile faces the lamp, so the warm light rimming the nose and forehead reads as a natural glow rather than a stare. This avoids the creepy intensity of a second inner gaze and keeps the composition ethically grounded: we see a life in progress, not an invasive look.

The inner figure will be drawn as a single filled silhouette path plus a separate rim light stroke. The profile head is being sketched with a nose wedge on the left, an upright or slightly curved back against a chair, and an arm reaching forward toward the table.

The inner figure's profile is being drafted as a single filled path with a nose wedge, a body outline, and a thick arm stroke. A chair will sit behind the figure. The artist is ready to write the full script and render.

The second line of the moral will be set in Georgia italic in lamp gold to read as a literary quotation rather than a greeting-card message. The dark, restrained image and absence of script type, hearts, drop shadows, or all-caps will keep the tone from becoming saccharine. The originality of the phrase "Leave them warmer than you found them" is also being questioned.

The phrase "Leave them warmer than you found them" is familiar but not exhausted. The image itself carries the metaphor, and the line serves as a handle for viewers. Alternatives like "They are lit from the inside" or "Don't put the light out" were considered and rejected.

The phrase "Leave them warmer than you found them" is kept as actionable and clear. A second line, "You are in there too," is added to include the viewer's own worth and prevent the poster from becoming self-righteous. A third line, a behavioral prompt in small tracked capitals, was considered but set aside to avoid text overload; it will be tested in the first render before inclusion.

The behavioral line is now included as a toggleable parameter. It defaults to small all-caps Georgia roman at y=1582, sized 11 with 2.5 letter spacing in #8a939c. The artist estimates it at roughly 400 pixels wide and considers it a quiet museum wall label that earns its place by turning art into a practical prompt for action.

A tiny window mark with glow will sit at the bottom center as a faint signature. A divider window will sit between the stanzas. The poster follows the golden rule of one idea, one image, and one memory. The script will be concise and clean.

The SVG will use an opaque background rectangle so it renders correctly on any surface. The viewBox and width/height attributes are being set for intrinsic sizing. A debug mode is unnecessary; the artist will render and inspect for coat-path bugs directly. Glow filters may be tested early if the full render looks wrong. Plant leaves will be drawn as ellipses with transforms.

Only one plant will be drawn, not two. The indigo curtain against amber is chosen for its rich depth. Wood grain on the frame was rejected as fussy; the double-frame structure is enough. The window construction is being drafted with a shadow rectangle on the coat, an outer dark frame, and a face layer.

The window face is being drawn as a wood-grained rectangle with a dark inner recess to sell depth. A linear gradient from #6b4a30 to #4a3220 will provide the wood tone, with top and left edge highlights at #c4a070 to suggest light from both inside and outside. The sill will project forward and carry a lighter top face.

The sill is being drawn as a three-dimensional polygon with a top face in #e0b080 and a front face in #a06840, plus a shadow line to sell depth. The plant will sit on the sill top. A thin gold inner lip is also being added.

The room interior is being clipped to a 178-by-208 rectangle at x=510, y=769. A translated group will keep the drawing coordinates clean.

The artist is pausing to verify SVG clip-path behavior. They need to confirm whether a clipPath on the same element as a transform applies in user space before or after the transform is applied, since this determines if the room interior will be clipped correctly.

The SVG spec confirms that clipPath units are independent of the element's transform. The room interior will be clipped by an outer group and drawn inside an inner group with a translate transform.

The room interior is being laid out at 178 by 208 pixels. The lamp will sit at x=70, the picture at (22, 36), and the table across y=142. The person head was initially placed at x=132 but shifted to x=118 so the chair back fits inside the right edge. The revised coordinates are now lamp x=70, person head at (118, 102) with radius 13, and chair back at x=128.

The table spans x=20 to x=108. The near cup sits at x=96 and the far cup at x=40, keeping the figure’s hands close to its own glass while the distant cup reads as a second place setting. Only two cups will be drawn.

The lamp shade will be the room's brightest element, followed by a radial gradient that darkens toward the right so the figure separates from the wall. A thin warm stroke on the left side of the profile will give it depth and readability. The artist is ready to write the code, render, and iterate, and will also add a crowd-drawing function with variety.

The older figure will carry a cane with a thin angled stroke and a small handle in dark gray. Their posture will be slightly bent forward. A child will hold the adult's hand, with windows at chest height for each figure. One person will also be drawn with a small bag, and another with a wider coat silhouette.

The crowd will avoid stereotyped ethnic markers to show universality. Heights, postures, and simple universal accessories like bags, canes, and caps will vary. A hooded figure will indicate the rain, while the hero’s face remains visible. The artist will keep the number of accessories minimal.

A seated figure will sit on a low step at the left, near a building. Their window remains bright and lit. The artist will not depict them as miserable; they are simply upright and resting. A simple crate or step will sit beneath them.

The step is being styled as a stoop at a building entrance so the seated figure reads as an ordinary neighbor rather than a victim. No one in the crowd will be drawn as a crisis figure; every figure is upright and ordinary, keeping the hero as an equal rather than a savior.

A soft warm ellipse will fall from the hero's window onto a nearby crowd member to suggest warmth reaching others. The value structure is being mapped: darkest for sky, vignette, hair and pupils; dark for coats, buildings and crowd bodies; mid for shadowed faces and street; light for warm face areas, moon and text; brightest for windows, lamp and catchlights.

The visual path will lead from the bright room window up to the figure’s eyes, then down to the text. The face stays mostly in shadow so the window can read as the jewel. Small catchlights in the eyes will anchor the gaze.

The window will glow so its warmth pools across the lower face and chin, with the eyes at the edge of that light. The artist is ready to write the script and will set overflow to hidden. Stars will be pre-generated to avoid the moon, clustered sparsely, and left with empty sky to honor the Japanese concept of ma.

About thirty stars will be hand-placed in a loose upper-left cluster, with a few near the moon and others isolated. The rain streaks will number ninety and avoid covering the face or window. A faint milky way will be added as a soft blurred ellipse at low opacity.

The milky way idea is dropped to avoid a smudge; stars and moon are enough. The moon will sit upper right at x=1040, y=118, facing left toward the figure with its crescent opening toward the person. The script will include a main function that writes the SVG and notes rendering. A preview render will be saved to poster.jpg at 800 pixels wide.

The face path may be simplified to a clean oval if the custom shape looks lumpy. A strict proportion checklist will guide the render: eyes halfway down the head, one eye-width apart, mouth halfway between nose and chin, ears between eye and nose lines, neck narrower than jaw, shoulders spanning roughly two to three head widths, window centered on chest, text not cramped, room readable, and the overall mood kept neutral and non-sentimental.

A ground reflection of the figure was considered but rejected to avoid muddying the silhouette. The artist is now writing the SVG file and organizing its structure carefully. Georgia font kerning is missing from the kern table, so manual overrides for specific pairs like "To", "Wa", and "Yo" will be added if spacing looks uneven.

Manual kerning overrides for Georgia are being deferred until after the full poster is rendered, since default sidebearings already look acceptable. The italic "in there" was confirmed to have a nice humanist feel. The poster builder script is now being written.

Building windows will stay warm or dark only. A cool blue window would distract from the warmth-as-life metaphor. Dark windows simply indicate unoccupied rooms. The artist is also considering a thin chimney or antenna.

Buildings will use simple rectangles with setbacks, plus one stepped roof and one sloped triangle for variety. Windows will be hand-placed rather than randomly generated, with only a few bright ones echoing the hero window to avoid visual clutter.

Eight to ten small lit windows will be placed across the city, each about seven by nine pixels. Roughly twenty dark windows will sit at low opacity to create subtle facade rhythm, using a slightly lighter gray than the buildings so they remain atmospheric rather than invisible.

Reflections of lit building windows will appear as soft vertical strokes in the street, with a taller streak for the hero. A faint foreground bokeh was considered but rejected to keep the illustration style. A small colophon line in uppercase Georgia at 12 pixels with letter-spacing 2.2 and color #7d8792 will sit at the bottom; it may be dropped if the render looks too busy.

The colophon line is finalized as a ritual phrase in small caps: "Before the harsh word, the turned back, the raised hand." Punctuation is chosen to keep the main lines flowing; "Someone is home" and "Leave them warmer" carry no period, while "in there." and "You are in there too." do. Italic optical centering will be adjusted because italics lean right.

Italic lines will be nudged left by four to eight pixels via an `dx` parameter. A render helper using rsvg-convert and ffmpeg will let the artist iterate quickly. The first version will stay a still image to avoid animation bloat. The chest-window, inner-lamp face lighting, and wet reflection leading to the words are being treated as the poster’s unique visual signature.

The artist will use small rounded rectangles for the eye catchlights rather than circles. Rectangles better mimic actual window reflections and fit the chest-window theme.

The left eye catchlight will be a 3×3.5 pixel rounded rectangle at the lower-center of the iris, filled with #ffe0a8. A smaller blue circle catchlight will sit near the upper-right of the iris. The artist decided against adding a thin warmth arc across the lower iris to avoid making the eyes look busy or insect-like. Eye proportions were verified as standard: roughly 44 pixels wide for a 280-pixel head, with a matching inter-eye gap.

Face coordinates are now fixed: head top at 250, chin at 575, eye line at 415, left eye center at 548, 418, right eye center at 652, 418, mouth at 600, 515, and nose tip at 600, 478. These will be constants so they can be nudged. The first face draft will likely need correction. Eyebrows will sit about 28 pixels apart with each brow roughly 48 pixels wide to avoid a unibrow.

Inner brows will stay level and relaxed, ending above the inner eye corners to avoid a worried or angry look. The SVG will include title and description metadata. Crowd windows will use a dark frame behind a warm rectangle, though the thin border may be too muddy at small scale.

content.text: The type outlines cleanly. Next I’ll build the poster itself: one person in the rain, a lit room where their chest is, and a line people can actually use.

arguments.content:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Someone is home in there.

A poster for the moment before you harm, dismiss, or pass someone by.
The figure is ordinary and upright — an equal, not a victim. The window
in the chest is a room, not a wound: framed, domestic, lit from within.
"""

import math
import os
import random
import subprocess
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(__file__))
from fontpath import load_font, text_path

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
FONT_DIR = "/System/Library/Fonts/Supplemental"
ROMAN = load_font(os.path.join(FONT_DIR, "Georgia.ttf"))
ITALIC = load_font(os.path.join(FONT_DIR, "Georgia Italic.ttf"))

W, H = 1200, 1600


def svg_text(font, text, size, x, y, fill, anchor="middle", tracking=0, dx=0, opacity=1):
    extra = f'opacity="{opacity:.3f}"' if opacity < 1 else ""
    element, width = text_path(
        font, text, size, x + dx, y, anchor=anchor, fill=fill,
        letter_spacing=tracking, extra=extra,
    )
    return element, width


def building(x, y, w, h, fill, windows, lit):
    """Simple facade. windows is a list of (rx, ry) relative lit or dark."""
    parts = [f'<rect x="{x}" y="{y}" width="{w}" height="{h}" fill="{fill}"/>']
    # slight lighter cornice
    parts.append(
        f'<rect x="{x}" y="{y}" width="{w}" height="3" fill="#243044" opacity="0.7"/>'
    )
    for wx, wy, on in windows:
        if on:
            parts.append(
                f'<rect x="{x+wx}" y="{y+wy}" width="8" height="10" rx="0.5" fill="#ffc98a"/>'
            )
            parts.append(
                f'<rect x="{x+wx}" y="{y+wy}" width="8" height="4" fill="#ffe6c0" opacity="0.85"/>'
            )
        else:
            parts.append(
                f'<rect x="{x+wx}" y="{y+wy}" width="7" height="9" fill="#1c2633" opacity="0.9"/>'
            )
    return "\n".join(parts)


def crowd_figure(cx, feet, h, kind="adult", light=1.0, hood=False):
    """A small person, dark, with a lit room at the chest. Dignity, no caricature."""
    if kind == "child":
        head_r = h * 0.20
        body_w = h * 0.30
    elif kind == "elder":
        head_r = h * 0.155
        body_w = h * 0.34
    else:
        head_r = h * 0.155
        body_w = h * 0.30
    head_cy = feet - h + head_r * 1.05
    if kind == "elder":
        head_cy += h * 0.04  # slight forward stoop, still upright enough to be proud
    shoulder_y = head_cy + head_r * 0.85
    body_top = shoulder_y - head_r * 0.15
    hem = feet
    left = cx - body_w
    right = cx + body_w
    # coat
    coat = (
        f"M {cx:.1f} {body_top:.1f} "
        f"C {left+body_w*0.3:.1f} {body_top:.1f}, {left:.1f} {shoulder_y:.1f}, {left-2:.1f} {shoulder_y+h*0.18:.1f} "
        f"C {left-4:.1f} {shoulder_y+h*0.42:.1f}, {left+2:.1f} {hem-h*0.08:.1f}, {left+body_w*0.35:.1f} {hem:.1f} "
        f"L {right-body_w*0.35:.1f} {hem:.1f} "
        f"C {right-2:.1f} {hem-h*0.08:.1f}, {right+4:.1f} {shoulder_y+h*0.42:.1f}, {right+2:.1f} {shoulder_y+h*0.18:.1f} "
        f"C {right:.1f} {shoulder_y:.1f}, {right-body_w*0.3:.1f} {body_top:.1f}, {cx:.1f} {body_top:.1f} Z"
    )
    head = f'<circle cx="{cx:.1f}" cy="{head_cy:.1f}" r="{head_r:.1f}" fill="#141b26"/>'
    hood_el = ""
    if hood:
        hood_el = (
            f'<path d="M {cx-head_r*0.9:.1f} {head_cy+2:.1f} '
            f'C {cx-head_r:.1f} {head_cy-head_r*1.3:.1f}, {cx+head_r:.1f} {head_cy-head_r*1.3:.1f}, '
            f'{cx+head_r*0.9:.1f} {head_cy+2:.1f} Z" fill="#101722"/>'
        )
    # window
    ww, wh = max(4.5, body_w * 0.42), max(6, h * 0.09)
    wx = cx - ww / 2
    wy = shoulder_y + h * 0.10
    win_op = 0.15 + 0.85 * light
    window = (
        f'<g opacity="{win_op:.3f}">'
        f'<rect x="{wx-0.6:.1f}" y="{wy-0.6:.1f}" width="{ww+1.2:.1f}" height="{wh+1.6:.1f}" fill="#2a2118"/>'
        f'<rect x="{wx:.1f}" y="{wy:.1f}" width="{ww:.1f}" height="{wh:.1f}" fill="#ffc27a"/>'
        f'<rect x="{wx:.1f}" y="{wy:.1f}" width="{ww:.1f}" height="{wh*0.42:.1f}" fill="#ffe6c2"/>'
        f'</g>'
    )
    # tiny ground reflection
    ref = (
        f'<ellipse cx="{cx:.1f}" cy="{feet+7:.1f}" rx="{ww:.1f}" ry="3.2" fill="#ffb060" '
        f'opacity="{0.18*light:.3f}"/>'
    )
    return (
        f'<g>'
        f'<path d="{coat}" fill="#141b26"/>'
        f'{head}{hood_el}{window}{ref}'
        f'</g>'
    )


def cane(x, y, h):
    return (
        f'<path d="M {x:.1f} {y:.1f} L {x+6:.1f} {y+h:.1f}" stroke="#5a6570" stroke-width="1.4" '
        f'stroke-linecap="round" fill="none"/>'
        f'<path d="M {x-3:.1f} {y:.1f} L {x+2:.1f} {y:.1f}" stroke="#5a6570" stroke-width="1.6" '
        f'stroke-linecap="round"/>'
    )


def stars():
    rng = random.Random(11)
    pts = []
    # loose cluster, upper left, and a few scattered — not a uniform field
    for _ in range(26):
        pts.append((rng.uniform(40, 520), rng.uniform(28, 240), rng.uniform(0.4, 1.15), rng.uniform(0.35, 0.9)))
    for _ in range(10):
        pts.append((rng.uniform(760, 1160), rng.uniform(36, 220), rng.uniform(0.35, 0.9), rng.uniform(0.25, 0.7)))
    for _ in range(8):
        pts.append((rng.uniform(80, 1120), rng.uniform(240, 520), rng.uniform(0.3, 0.7), rng.uniform(0.15, 0.4)))
    out = []
    for x, y, r, o in pts:
        out.append(f'<circle cx="{x:.1f}" cy="{y:.1f}" r="{r:.2f}" fill="#e7eef8" opacity="{o:.2f}"/>')
        if r > 0.95:
            out.append(
                f'<path d="M {x:.1f} {y-3.2:.1f} L {x:.1f} {y+3.2:.1f} M {x-3.2:.1f} {y:.1f} L {x+3.2:.1f} {y:.1f}" '
                f'stroke="#e7eef8" stroke-width="0.4" opacity="{o*0.7:.2f}"/>'
            )
    return "\n".join(out)


def rain(seed, n, x0, x1, y0, y1, opacity, length=16):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    parts = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = rng.uniform(x0, x1)
        y = rng.uniform(y0, y1)
        parts.append(
            f'<line x1="{x:.1f}" y1="{y:.1f}" x2="{x+5:.1f}" y2="{y+length:.1f}" '
            f'stroke="#c5d0dc" stroke-width="0.8" opacity="{opacity:.3f}" stroke-linecap="round"/>'
        )
    return "\n".join(parts)


def build():
    parts = []
    A = parts.append

    A('<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>')
    A(f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" width="{W}" height="{H}" viewBox="0 0 {W} {H}">')
    A("<title>Someone is home in there</title>")
    A(
        "<desc>A person stands in the rain at night, upright and calm, meeting your eyes. "
        "Set into their chest is a real window with a wooden frame and a sill. Through it, "
        "a warmly lit room: a lamp, two cups on a table, a plant, and someone sitting at home, "
        "turned toward their own light. The same warmth is caught in the standing person's eyes. "
        "Around them on the wet street, other people — a child, an elder, neighbors — each carry "
        "a small lit window. The words read: Someone is home in there. Leave them warmer than "
        "you found them. You are in there too.</desc>"
    )

    A("""<defs>
    <linearGradient id="sky" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#07090e"/>
      <stop offset="38%" stop-color="#101722"/>
      <stop offset="62%" stop-color="#161e2a"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#0b0e14"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <radialGradient id="lampPool" cx="50%" cy="46%" r="48%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#f0a24a" stop-opacity="0.30"/>
      <stop offset="32%" stop-color="#c46a28" stop-opacity="0.10"/>
      <stop offset="68%" stop-color="#c46a28" stop-opacity="0.02"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#c46a28" stop-opacity="0"/>
    </radialGradient>
    <radialGradient id="vignette" cx="50%" cy="40%" r="72%">
      <stop offset="55%" stop-color="#000" stop-opacity="0"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#000" stop-opacity="0.62"/>
    </radialGradient>
    <linearGradient id="faceGrad" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#2a3344"/>
      <stop offset="42%" stop-color="#3a343c"/>
      <stop offset="70%" stop-color="#5c433c"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#7a5648"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="neckGrad" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#4a3834"/>
      <stop offset="55%" stop-color="#3a2c2c"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#241c22"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <radialGradient id="coatGrad" cx="50%" cy="42%" r="62%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#2a241f"/>
      <stop offset="42%" stop-color="#1a2130"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#121820"/>
    </radialGradient>
    <linearGradient id="wood" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#7a5340"/>
      <stop offset="40%" stop-color="#4e3426"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#3a261c"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <radialGradient id="roomWall" cx="42%" cy="28%" r="75%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#ffe0b0"/>
      <stop offset="45%" stop-color="#f0b56e"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#d4894e"/>
    </radialGradient>
    <linearGradient id="floorG" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#c48448"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#8a542e"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="reflect" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#ffb25c" stop-opacity="0.42"/>
      <stop offset="35%" stop-color="#e88840" stop-opacity="0.14"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#e88840" stop-opacity="0"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <linearGradient id="street" x1="0" y1="0" x2="0" y2="1">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#141b26"/>
      <stop offset="30%" stop-color="#10151e"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#0c1016"/>
    </linearGradient>
    <filter id="blur18" x="-60%" y="-60%" width="220%" height="220%">
      <feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="18"/>
    </filter>
    <filter id="blur8" x="-40%" y="-40%" width="180%" height="180%">
      <feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="7"/>
    </filter>
    <filter id="blur3" x="-30%" y="-30%" width="160%" height="160%">
      <feGaussianBlur stdDeviation="2.4"/>
    </filter>
    <clipPath id="roomClip">
      <rect x="518" y="778" width="164" height="196"/>
    </clipPath>
    <clipPath id="posterClip">
      <rect width="1200" height="1600"/>
    </clipPath>
  </defs>""")

    A('<g clip-path="url(#posterClip)">')

    # sky
    A('<rect width="1200" height="1600" fill="url(#sky)"/>')
    A('<rect width="1200" height="1600" fill="url(#lampPool)"/>')
    A(stars())

    # moon — crescent facing the figure
    A('<circle cx="1042" cy="118" r="46" fill="#d5e2f2" opacity="0.10" filter="url(#blur18)"/>')
    A("""<mask id="crescent">
      <circle cx="1036" cy="124" r="26" fill="white"/>
      <circle cx="1050" cy="112" r="22" fill="black"/>
    </mask>
    <circle cx="1036" cy="124" r="26" fill="#f4f7fb" mask="url(#crescent)"/>""")

    # distant buildings, framing the head but leaving sky around the face
    A(building(0, 610, 78, 430, "#0e141c", [
        (18, 40, True), (46, 70, False), (22, 120, False), (48, 160, True),
        (20, 220, False), (44, 250, False), (24, 310, True),
    ], True))
    A(building(62, 690, 118, 350, "#121924", [
        (16, 36, False), (48, 36, True), (80, 36, False),
        (16, 90, False), (48, 90, False), (80, 90, True),
        (22, 150, True), (60, 160, False), (86, 200, False),
        (30, 230, False),
    ], True))
    A(building(168, 760, 96, 280, "#101722", [
        (14, 28, False), (42, 28, False), (68, 48, True),
        (16, 100, False), (48, 110, False), (20, 170, True),
    ], True))
    A(building(250, 820, 70, 220, "#0e141c", [
        (14, 30, True), (40, 70, False), (18, 120, False),
    ], True))

    A(building(900, 800, 88, 240, "#101722", [
        (14, 28, False), (44, 40, True), (18, 90, False), (50, 120, False),
        (22, 170, True),
    ], True))
    A(building(972, 680, 130, 360, "#121924", [
        (16, 30, True), (52, 30, False), (88, 30, False),
        (18, 84, False), (54, 84, True), (90, 90, False),
        (20, 150, False), (60, 160, False), (96, 150, True),
        (28, 220, True), (70, 230, False),
    ], True))
    A(building(1090, 590, 110, 450, "#0e141c", [
        (18, 36, False), (52, 50, True), (80, 36, False),
        (20, 110, True), (58, 120, False), (84, 160, False),
        (24, 200, False), (62, 220, True), (28, 290, False),
        (70, 320, True),
    ], True))

    # rain behind the figure
    A(rain(3, 110, 0, 1200, 0, 1100, 0.11, 15))

    # crowd — behind and beside the hero, each with a light
    # left cluster
    A(crowd_figure(48, 1035, 40, hood=True))
    A(crowd_figure(118, 1042, 58))
    A(crowd_figure(188, 1048, 78))
